analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal board that can shorten drug patents when companies charge excessive prices.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 2 cosponsors, was sent to two House committees and two subcommittees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a five-member Patented Medicine Prices Review Board inside the FDA. Each year, makers of patented prescription drugs would have to report their prices, production costs, and marketing costs. If the board found a company charging an excessive price — judged against its own past prices, similar drugs, prices in other countries, and executive pay — it could shorten that company's patent, cutting off the monopoly period that lets brand-name drugs sell without competition. Companies that kept prices in line could earn up to a 10% longer patent. The board would also tell federal agencies which drugs were overpriced and recommend cheaper substitutes.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, insurers, and government programs that pay for prescription drugs. Excessive-price findings could shorten patent terms, letting generic versions reach the market sooner and lowering what people and federal programs like Medicare and Medicaid pay.

how_it_helps.text: The board could shorten a drug patent's length when the patentee charges an excessive price, ending the monopoly sooner and opening the drug to generic competition.

The board would judge excessive prices against the company's own past prices, comparable drugs in the same therapeutic class, prices charged in other countries, production costs, and executive pay relative to line workers' pay.

The board would report annually to every federal agency that dispenses or pays for prescription drugs, listing drugs sold at excessive prices and recommending they not be dispensed or paid for, or be substituted with similar drugs priced lower.
Board members had to be experts in consumer advocacy, medicine, pharmacology, pharmacy, or drug reimbursement, and could not have worked in the pharmaceutical industry during the prior year.
Companies that avoided excessive prices for five years could apply for a patent extension of up to 10%, tying longer monopoly rights to price restraint.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers holding patents. Their patents could be cut shorter for charging excessive prices, they would face annual reporting of prices, costs, and executive compensation, and the board could compel testimony and documents by subpoena.

drawbacks.text: Linking drug prices to patent length is a blunt tool: shortening a patent punishes an overcharging company but does not directly lower the price patients pay today — relief arrives only after the patent ends and generics enter.

The bill gave the board wide discretion to define 'excessive' and set penalty sizes, which pharmaceutical makers could be expected to challenge as arbitrary and as effectively compelled price regulation through the patent system.

Patent terms are set under the patent laws administered by a separate system; moving control over their effective length to a new FDA board raised questions of consistency with international patent commitments and with the incentive the patent system provides for developing new drugs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who pay for prescription drugs — directly or through taxes and insurance premiums — the bill offered a real lever against high patented-drug prices: lose monopoly time if you overcharge, gain a little if you don't. The honest costs are on the innovation side: shorter effective patents reduce the payoff for developing new drugs, and the board's broad discretion made outcomes hard to predict. It was a strong price-control design whose main flaw was that it never advanced far enough to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and split between two House committees, then sent to subcommittees in each, and sat there until the Congress ended with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the bill on July 2, 1992, late in the second session of the 102nd Congress, with two cosponsors (one Democrat, one Independent).
The same day, it was referred jointly to the House Judiciary and Energy and Commerce Committees.
Within a month it was sent to the Health and the Environment Subcommittee of Energy and Commerce and the Intellectual Property and Judicial Administration Subcommittee of Judiciary.
No further action appears in the record; the bill died in committee when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers kept their full patent terms and faced no new price reporting or excessive-price penalties. Patients continued paying prevailing patented-drug prices.

for.name: Rep. Fortney Pete Stark
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 2, 1992, to create a board that could shorten drug patents for excessive pricing.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to its Health and the Environment Subcommittee, and took no further action; no hearing or vote occurred.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the joint referral, sent it to its Intellectual Property and Judicial Administration Subcommittee, and took no further action; no hearing or vote occurred.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows the split; its three sponsors were one Democrat and one Independent.

industries.note: Patent terms are the source of brand-name drug companies' monopoly pricing power, so a board that could cut patent terms for excessive prices directly threatened their revenue. The bill also would have required annual disclosure of prices, costs, and executive pay, and empowered the board to subpoena records.

Shorter patent terms and board recommendations that federal agencies substitute lower-priced drugs would hasten generic entry and expand generic sales. Cheaper substitutes would lower costs for patients and federal programs.

industries.industry: Federal health payers (Medicare, Medicaid, agencies dispensing drugs)
industries.note: The board would hand federal agencies an annual list of overpriced drugs with recommendations against paying for them, giving government programs a tool to steer spending toward lower-priced equivalents.
